subtitle: Pandas' answer to a SQL join.

eyebrow: A clean merge: regions to warehouses
code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")

warehouses = pd.DataFrame({
    "region": ["West", "East", "South", "North"],
    "warehouse_city": ["Reno, NV", "Newark, NJ", "Atlanta, GA", "Minneapolis, MN"],
})

orders_with_warehouse = df.merge(warehouses, on="region", how="left")
caption: merge(on="region", how="left") is a LEFT JOIN. All 4 regions match, so this adds a column and loses nothing — still 20 rows.

eyebrow: When the merge key doesn't fully match
code:
priority = pd.DataFrame({
    "category": ["Footwear", "Camping", "Packs"],  # Accessories missing on purpose
    "ship_priority": ["Standard", "Standard", "Standard"],
})

left = df.merge(priority, on="category", how="left")
print(left["ship_priority"].isna().sum())   # 4
print(len(left))                              # 20
caption: how="left" always keeps every row. The 4 Accessories orders just get NaN — no match, but no row lost either.
inner keeps only rows matching on both sides — all 4 Accessories orders disappear, with no NaN warning sign at all.

steps.label: LEFT
steps.sub: Keeps every row from your main data; gaps become NaN

steps.label: INNER
steps.sub: Keeps only rows matching both sides — can drop rows silently

steps.label: RIGHT
steps.sub: Keeps every row from the other DataFrame (rare)

steps.label: OUTER
steps.sub: Keeps every row from both sides, matched or not
